newsitem.title: HONG KONG: US pension funds to take closer look at China, HK.
newsitem.headline: US pension funds to take closer look at China, HK.

text.p: U.S. pension fund managers representing US$250 billion in funds will visit Hong Kong this week to take a closer look at investment opportunities in Hong Kong and, especially, in China, the sponsor said on Tuesday.
The trip is sponsored by Hong Kong brokerage company Mansion House. Co-sponsors include a number of U.S. investment banks, Mansion House adviser Henry Luk said in an interview.

A 30-member delegation from the California Public Employees Retirement System (Calpers) will meet investment managers, company executives, the Hong Kong Airport Authority and Chinese and Hong Kong government officials starting on January 12.
Representatives from other U.S. state treasuries also are expected to attend.
In Hong Kong, the agenda includes discussions with Chief Executive-designate Tung Chee-hwa, Chief Secretary Anson Chan and Financial Secretary Donald Tsang.
The leader of the California delegation, State Treasurer Matthew Fong, took a similar trip to Hong Kong and southern China last August that also was sponsored by Mansion House.
Ohio State Treasurer Kenneth Blackwell and Connecticut State Treasurer Christopher Burnham also participated in the August trip, Mansion House chairman Evans Lowe said.
U.S. pension funds, many of which already are invested in Asia through index funds, are seeking managers with expertise in China markets to direct their investments, Lowe said.
Pension administrators are particularly keen to engage investment managers that understand the way business works in both the U.S. and in China, he said.

"In this part of the world, you need to spend time to understand the culture, the backround and the way to do business," said Hong Kong-born Lowe, who spent 20 years in the United States. He returned about two decades ago.
U.S. pension funds had only about five percent of their funds invested overseas in 1993, a far smaller percentage than funds of other industrialized countries, Lowe said.

"If U.S. private pension funds were to increase their foreign assets from five percent to 20 percent they would need to deploy about US$1.5 trillion dollars overseas," Lowe told pension fund investors at a forum in New York last November.

Calpers already is taking a bet on Asian growth through a US$250 million pledge made last December to sponsor an Asian Development Bank fund to promote private sector involvement in infrastructure projects in the region.

Mansion House's Luk said U.S. fund managers are eager to explore opportunities in China, despite occasionally cool relations between it and the U.S., on the view that in the long run it is in the interests of both countries to mend their differences.
Still, Mansion House is careful to recommend investments in China "that are unlikely to cause controversy," he said.
